newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Dresdner-NFF commodity index up on beef, wool.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Dresdner-NFF commodity index up on beef, wool.

text.p: A significant increase in beef and wool prices helped up push up Australian rural commodity prices this month but a stronger Australian dollar whittled away most of the gains, Dresdner Australia Ltd and the National Farmers Federation (NFF) said on Monday.

The Dresdner commodity price index, measured in Special Drawing Rights (SDR) terms, rose 3.2 percent in March and was 7.5 percent above the year-earlier level, Dresdner-NFF said in their International Commodity Price Review monthly.
But in Australian dollar terms, the index fell 0.3 percent in March due to a stronger local currency, they said.

Dresdner-NFF said the rural price index in SDR terms rose 4.7 percent in March, making a 10.9 percent rise over the year-earlier level, but rose only 1.1 percent in Australian dollar terms over the month.
The rise was largely due to stronger beef prices while wool, sorghum, rice and cotton also rose.

"Beef prices were driven by a strong improvement in U.S. manufactured beef prices, as a result of lower meat production and improved demand, as well as news that the McDonald's chain had launched a 55 U.S. cents beef patty sandwich in the U.S.," NFF economic policy director Todd Ritchie said in a statement,
But Dresdner-NFF said beef prices are expected to come under renewed pressure in the coming months as U.S. feed cattle production peaks.
"Wool prices also moved higher during the month, with the eastern markert indicator reaching its higher level since November 15, 1995," Ritchie said.
"There was a lift in demand from Japan, China and Taiwan and a seasonal slowdown in new supply," he said.
The non-rural index rose 2.5 percent in March in SDR terms, to stand 5.6 percent above the year-ago level, but declined 1.0 percent in Australian dollar terms in March.

"The underlying demand for commodity exports is rising, as the Japanese economy continues to post solid growth and the U.S. continues to outperform expectations," Dresdner chief economist Rob Henderson said in the statement.
"Rising world prices of commodities and the market perception that the Reserve Bank's easing cycle is over saw the A$ jump to 80 U.S. cents in March," he said.
"The currency could rise further on the favourable world demand outlook, although some initial weakness is possible if the Federal Reserve increases U.S. rates," he added.
